chunks: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when he had been asked about a man who slaughters and the knife hastens and cuts off the head. He said: 'The swift slaughter — there is no problem with eating it if it was not done deliberately.'

key_terms.الذَّكَاة: The Islamic act of ritual slaughter (dhakat/tadhkiya) — rendering an animal lawful for consumption by cutting the throat with a sharp blade while invoking God's name
key_terms.الْوَحِيَّة: Swift, intense, complete — describes slaughter where the motion was so rapid it resulted in full decapitation
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: No problem, no harm, permissible — standard Shia jurisprudential phrase indicating permissibility

ai.seo_question: Is meat permissible if the head was accidentally completely severed during Islamic slaughter?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addressed a question about an accidental over-cutting during animal slaughter, where the knife moved so fast that the animal's head was completely severed. He ruled that such meat is permissible to eat (halal), provided that the slaughterer did not intend to cut the head off entirely — this ruling hinges on the concept of 'al-dhakat al-wahiyya' (the swift/complete slaughter), affirming that unintentional complete decapitation during slaughter does not invalidate the animal's permissibility for consumption. This legal clarification would have been of practical importance for communities where slaughter was a daily act requiring jurisprudential guidance.
